query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for structural use under extreme-temperature conditions, what single intervention could improve high-temperature oxygen resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the temperature, atmosphere, and exposure conditions under which it should work, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a single, severe surface deformation treatment that refines the near‐surface grain structure of a refractory high‐entropy alloy (such as MoNbTaTiW) will improve its high‐temperature oxygen resistance by enabling faster and more uniform formation of a protective alumina/chromia scale.
generation.material_initial_state: A refractory high‐entropy alloy (e.g., MoNbTaTiW) with a conventional, coarse-grained microstructure and alloying elements (such as Al and Cr at baseline levels) that in the untreated state form non-uniform oxide scales upon high-temperature oxidation.
generation.intervention: Perform a localized severe plastic deformation process (e.g., friction stir processing) on the alloy surface to generate an ultrafine-grained layer.
generation.conditions: Isothermal oxidation in dry air at 1100 °C for 100 hours.
generation.structural_mediator: An ultrafine-grained surface layer with a high density of grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: The enhanced grain boundary density accelerates the diffusion of protective elements (e.g., Al and Cr) to the surface, promoting the rapid nucleation and growth of continuous and adherent alumina/chromia scales that restrict further oxygen ingress.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated alloy, the treated specimens will exhibit a significantly lower mass gain (e.g., an improvement on the order of ~30–40% reduction in oxidation rate) and demonstrate a more uniform, continuous protective oxide scale upon post-oxidation microstructural analysis.
generation.baseline: Untreated refractory high-entropy alloy specimens with coarse-grained surfaces that develop less uniform and partly spalled oxide layers, resulting in higher mass gain during oxidation tests.
generation.boundary: This improvement is expected under high-temperature, dry air conditions for up to about 100 hours; the effectiveness under varying atmospheres, extreme thermal cycling, or very long exposure times remains to be established.
generation.uncertainty: The hypothesis extends the beneficial effect of microstructural refinement on oxidation resistance observed in conventional HEAs (PMC9026100::web::003::introduction) to refractory HEAs, and combines it with data indicating that refractory HEAs form protective oxides (PMC6513993::web::015::discussion). However, the magnitude of enhancement in refractory systems is uncertain due to their inherently sluggish diffusion kinetics and complex oxide formation behavior.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of MoNbTaTiW refractory HEA specimens: one group undergoes friction stir processing (or an equivalent severe surface deformation method) to produce an ultrafine-grained surface layer, and the other group remains untreated. Subject both groups to isothermal oxidation at 1100 °C in dry air for 100 hours under identical conditions. After oxidation, assess mass gain and perform detailed microstructural analysis (using SEM, TEM, and XRD) to characterize the oxide scale morphology and continuity.
measurements: Mass gain per unit area (e.g., mg/cm²) using thermogravimetric analysis
Grain size measurement of the surface layer before and after oxidation
Morphology and continuity of the oxide scale via SEM/TEM
Phase identification of oxides via XRD
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the ultrafine-grained (processed) specimens do not show a statistically significant reduction (e.g., ≮30% improvement in mass gain) and fail to exhibit a more uniform and continuous protective oxide layer compared to the untreated specimens under these conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Thus, there is a need to develop advanced materials with superior surface oxidation resistance and improved mechanical properties at high temperature. High entropy alloys (HEAs) represent an emerging class of advanced materials for high temperature applications owing to their promising mechanical properties, namely, outstanding structural strength, high hardness,, enhanced fracture toughness, prominent fatigue resistance, and remarkable oxidation and corrosion resistance. The oxidation behavior of HEAs has been extensively reported. Kim et al. examined the oxidation behavior of a Cr–Mn–Fe–Co–Ni HEA system for a duration of 24 h at three different temperatures, 900, 1000, and 1100 °C, revealing mass gain of 1.76, 4.45, and 9.08 mg/cm2, respectively. Nong et al. studied the high temperature oxidation behavior of AlCrFeNiTiMnx (where x = 0 and 0.5) HEAs at 900 °C for 100 h and probed the poor oxidation resistance of Mn containing alloys, which was attributed to the adverse effect of Mn-rich oxides.
